I want to be upfront that this is a recommendation with a shelf life: if utilisation work stalls or if demand grows faster than our current forecast, the case for buying flips quickly, and we should treat this as a reversible, low-commitment posture rather than a strategic bet against expansion.

**Where we actually are**

Our four inference nodes currently average somewhere between 30 and 40 percent utilisation, with batch jobs pushing individual cards to saturation overnight while interactive work sits idle much of the day. That gap is the whole argument. When we feel capacity pressure, what we usually feel is *temporal* contention — the demo cluster is busy at 2pm because the training queue is also busy at 2pm — not an absolute shortage of FLOPs across the week. Buying hardware to fix a scheduling problem is the most expensive possible fix, because the purchase price is only the beginning: there is colocation or power cost, a maintenance tail, and, less obviously, an operational surface that grows with every device we own. Every additional node is something that can fail, needs driver updates, and quietly consumes someone's attention.

**Cost, honestly framed**

The quote we got for two additional nodes is roughly equivalent to eleven months of a mid-level engineer. That is the real comparison, not hardware versus nothing. If we buy, we are implicitly saying that an engineer's time is better spent elsewhere than on the scheduling and queueing work that might make the purchase unnecessary. If we don't buy, we are implicitly saying that an engineer's time *is* well spent on that work. Both positions are defensible; what matters is which one we can defend with evidence. Right now we have anecdotes about contention and a utilisation dashboard nobody fully trusts. Before spending capital, we should be able to say, with numbers, what fraction of our demand is genuinely unschedulable.

**Latency is the honest counterargument**

I want to give the strongest case for buying its due. Utilisation improvements are, in practice, latency improvements for batch and throughput workloads, but they do relatively little for tail latency on interactive inference. If our product requirement is p99 response times under load, queueing smarter can only go so far; at some point you need headroom that exists even when everything else is busy. The risk of the utilisation-first path is that we spend a quarter optimising and still end up buying hardware, having spent both time and money. That outcome is possible, and I don't want to pretend otherwise. But note what it costs us: mostly engineer time on work — better queueing, workload consolidation, honest capacity telemetry — that has value even if we do eventually buy. Sunk optimisation effort is not wasted; it compounds with whatever hardware we own.

**Reliability and opportunity cost**

There is also a reliability argument that cuts both ways. More nodes mean more redundancy, which is genuinely valuable — we currently have a single point of failure in the sense that losing one node costs us a third of capacity. But redundancy bought through expansion also means more components that can fail and more failure modes to debug. Meanwhile, the opportunity cost of the purchase is concrete: the same capital could fund a contractor for the data pipeline work we keep deferring, or simply extend our runway. Deferring a purchase is not free of risk, but it keeps options open, and options have value when our demand forecast has error bars as wide as they currently do.

**Reversibility**

This is the part I weight most heavily. Buying hardware is close to irreversible at our scale — depreciated machines are hard to resell and impossible to unown. Improving utilisation is almost perfectly reversible: if the scheduling work doesn't deliver, we've lost a quarter and gained telemetry, and we can make the purchase with better information. When one path is reversible and the other is not, and the evidence is ambiguous, the reversible path should win.

**What I'm asking for**

Agreement to spend the next eight to ten weeks on utilisation: fix the telemetry, consolidate the batch queue, and pilot time-slicing on the inference nodes. We reconvene with real numbers. If contention persists after that, I will be the first to argue for the purchase — with data this time, and with the confidence that we're buying capacity we actually need rather than capacity we failed to schedule.

The framing we've been using — "should we buy more hardware or should we use what we have better?" — sounds like a clean either/or, but the honest answer is that these options have very different risk profiles, and the right choice depends on which failure mode we're more willing to live with.

Let me start with the case for buying. Our inference cluster has been saturating above 85% during peak hours for six consecutive weeks, and queue times on the batch pipeline have crept from minutes to nearly an hour. When we hit saturation, latency degrades in ways our users actually notice: p95 response times on the assistant endpoint have roughly doubled since the spring. If our product roadmap holds — and the search relevance work plus the two internal pilots scheduled for next quarter are reasonably firm commitments — demand will outstrip supply by early Q3. Buying two more nodes now would cost us roughly the equivalent of one engineer-year, which is real money for a team our size, but it would restore headroom immediately and buy us perhaps eighteen months of comfortable growth.

The case for improving utilisation is less glamorous but worth taking seriously. Our measured utilisation is misleading. A good chunk of that 85% is idle-but-reserved capacity: notebooks left attached to GPUs over weekends, batch jobs scheduled with generous memory footprints "just in case," and a staging environment that mirrors production sizing out of habit rather than need. An honest audit suggests we could recover 20 to 30 percentage points of effective capacity through scheduling discipline, better bin-packing of models, and quantisation of the two largest serving workloads. That work is mostly engineering time we'd spend anyway on operational hygiene, and unlike hardware, it compounds — the tooling we build for scheduling will keep paying off.

So why am I leaning toward buying, despite the obvious appeal of the cheaper option? Three reasons. First, latency. Utilisation improvements reduce queueing on average, but they don't change the physics of peak load. If we run hot at 90%+ effective utilisation after optimisation, tail latency gets *worse*, not better, because we've removed the slack that absorbs bursts. Our users tolerate slow Tuesdays; they don't tolerate flaky Fridays. Second, opportunity cost. The engineering time to do utilisation work properly is two to three months of senior attention, and that same attention is exactly what our roadmap work needs. We would be trading product velocity for infrastructure tidiness, and at our stage I don't think that trade is right. Third, reversibility. Hardware is a lumpy but largely reversible commitment — nodes can be repurposed, resold, or reallocated to training jobs if demand disappoints. The scheduling and tooling work, once embedded in how the team operates, is much harder to unwind if it turns out we misjudged demand.

That said, I want to be honest about the uncertainty here, because it cuts both ways. Our demand forecast rests on the assumption that the Q3 pilots convert to production workloads, and pilot conversion rates historically run about fifty percent. If they don't convert, we'll have bought capacity we don't need and will carry the depreciation. Hardware prices are also drifting down as newer generations ship, which means buying now has a real cost in foregone future price-performance. And there's a scenario — a serious one — where a major model release changes our serving economics entirely and makes both our current fleet and any new purchase partially obsolete.

My recommendation, then, is a split decision weighted toward purchase: commit to the two nodes now, but pair the purchase with a bounded, two-week utilisation audit — not the full three-month optimisation programme — to catch the obvious waste (weekend reservations, oversized staging) without diverting senior engineers from roadmap work. This hedges both failure modes: we protect latency and delivery dates if demand materialises, and we recover cheap capacity if it doesn't. I'd rather spend a modest amount on insurance in both directions than bet the quarter on a single forecast.

I'm open to being argued out of this, particularly on the timing of the purchase. Please come Thursday with objections.

Our inference fleet sits above 80% peak utilisation during business hours, queue times for batch jobs have crept into the overnight window, and every new project this year has started with someone asking whether there's a GPU free. Hardware is also getting more expensive to rent in the cloud, and there's a genuine strategic argument for owning capacity we control end to end. If our workload keeps growing at anything like its current rate, we will need more silicon eventually. The question is whether "eventually" means this quarter.

The case for improving utilisation first rests on three observations. The first is that our measured utilisation is misleading. That 80% figure counts allocated time, not useful compute. A meaningful fraction of our allocation is held by idle notebooks, oversized reservations that were never resized after experiments ended, and batch jobs scheduled at conservative batch sizes. Industry experience, and our own spot checks, suggest that a fleet that looks 80% busy is often doing 40–50% useful work. If we can move true utilisation by even fifteen points through better scheduling, right-sizing, and a shared queue with preemption, we buy ourselves the equivalent of several new cards without spending capital.

The second observation is about reversibility, and I think this is the most important consideration. Money spent on hardware is largely spent. Cards depreciate, rack space is committed, and if our workload mix shifts — say, toward smaller models or toward a hosted API for the long tail — we own machines that no longer fit the problem. Money and time spent on scheduling software, monitoring, and quota policy is mostly recoverable: the tooling has value even if we later buy hardware, and the discipline it enforces has value regardless. When two options have similar expected benefit, the reversible one is almost always the better bet, and these options do not have similar reversibility.

The third observation is opportunity cost. The team is small, and the engineering weeks we'd spend on utilisation are weeks not spent on product work. That cost is real and I don't want to pretend otherwise. But the alternative also consumes the team: procuring, racking, integrating, and operating new hardware is not free, and it lands on the same people. The difference is that the utilisation work produces durable capability — better observability, a real scheduler, honest capacity metrics — while the purchase produces capacity whose value depends on assumptions we haven't yet tested.

On latency, the picture is mixed but not decisive. Our interactive inference latency is fine when the fleet is quiet and degrades at peak, which is a scheduling problem as much as a capacity problem. Adding hardware would mask it; better queueing and priority classes would fix it. If after the utilisation work we still see p99 latency violations at moderate load, that is strong evidence the constraint is genuinely physical, and the purchase case becomes much stronger.

I want to be honest about the uncertainty here. My claim that we can recover fifteen points of utilisation is an estimate, not a measurement, and utilisation projects have a way of stalling in organisational friction — nobody wants to give up a reservation they might need. There's also a risk that the exercise becomes an excuse to defer a decision we already know we'll have to make. To guard against that, I propose we treat this as a bounded commitment: a defined period of utilisation work with agreed metrics, after which we make the hardware decision with data rather than intuition. If the work stalls or the gains don't materialise, we buy, and we'll have lost little.

The failure mode I most want to avoid is buying hardware to solve a scheduling problem, then discovering in a year that we're running the same argument at a larger scale. Let's find out what we actually own before we buy more of it.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering leadership
**From:** Infrastructure team
**Re:** Inference capacity planning for the next two quarters

We've been asked to settle a question that has come up repeatedly in the last month: do we purchase additional local hardware to serve our model inference load, or do we invest in squeezing more out of the machines we already own? I want to lay out the reasoning as I see it, because the answer is less obvious than either the "just buy GPUs" or "just optimize" camps suggest, and the decision has consequences that will be hard to undo in either direction.

First, the cost picture. Our current fleet runs at roughly 45% average utilization, which sounds like a strong argument for optimization before procurement. But that number hides important variance. Utilization is high — often saturated — during business-hours batch work and nearly zero overnight and on weekends. The peak-to-trough ratio is what drives our pain: we queue jobs at 2pm and idle hardware at 2am. Buying more hardware would raise our baseline cost permanently: capital outlay, colocation power, cooling, and maintenance contracts that recur whether we use the capacity or not. Optimization work, by contrast, is mostly engineering time we'd spend anyway, though I want to be honest that "engineering time we'd spend anyway" is doing real work in that sentence. A serious batching and scheduling effort is probably two engineers for six to eight weeks, and those are weeks not spent on the product roadmap. That opportunity cost is real and should be priced into the comparison rather than waved away as free.

Second, latency. This is where the two options genuinely diverge. Better scheduling and batching improves throughput but tends to trade some latency for it — larger batches mean longer queueing for individual requests. Our interactive workloads are already close to our latency budget at peak, and I'm not confident that smarter batching alone keeps us inside it as traffic grows. Additional hardware, on the other hand, buys headroom directly: more concurrent capacity means shorter queues without the batching trade-off. If latency is a hard constraint rather than a soft target, that argues for hardware. If it's a soft target, it argues for optimization.

Third, reliability. Our current setup has a single point of failure we don't like to talk about: one of our four nodes carries disproportionate load, and if it fails during peak hours, we degrade visibly. More hardware improves redundancy as a side effect. Optimization does not — in fact, aggressive utilization tuning typically runs nodes hotter and closer to their limits, which can slightly worsen failure characteristics. We should not optimize our way into a more fragile system.

Fourth, and I think most importantly, reversibility. Buying hardware is a largely irreversible commitment. Reselling specialized accelerators recovers maybe half the purchase price, and the recurring costs lock us in for the life of the equipment. Optimization work is the opposite: it's reversible in the sense that if it fails, we've lost time but retained the option to buy hardware later, and much of what we'd build — better queueing, better observability, a real utilization dashboard — retains value regardless of which path we eventually take. Asymmetric bets where the cheap option preserves the expensive option are usually worth taking.

So my recommendation: invest in utilization first, but with a deadline and a tripwire. We should commit to a focused eight-week effort on scheduling, batching, and load balancing, with a concrete target — sustained utilization above 65% and peak latency holding within budget. If we hit the target, we've likely deferred hardware purchase by at least two quarters. If we miss it, or if latency degrades past acceptable thresholds along the way, we trigger the hardware purchase with the optimization work still banked as infrastructure we'd want anyway.

I want to acknowledge the uncertainty honestly. Our traffic forecast is shaky; if growth accelerates, optimization buys us time but not capacity, and we'd end up buying hardware later under time pressure, which is when bad procurement decisions happen. Conversely, if growth stalls, hardware bought now becomes a stranded cost. The optimization path is robust to both scenarios in a way the purchase path is not, and that robustness, more than any single number, is why I favor it.

Happy to walk through the utilization data and the latency measurements in detail at Thursday's review. I'd like a decision by end of month so the engineering work, if approved, can start at the beginning of the next sprint cycle.

**The case against buying is that we're not actually constrained by hardware — we're constrained by how we use it.** Our measured utilisation sits at 38% averaged across the fleet, with individual nodes ranging from 12% to 81%. That spread is the tell. We have batch jobs scheduled at midnight on the same nodes that serve interactive traffic at 2pm. We have models loaded into VRAM that get invoked twice a day. We have no shared queue, no priority classes, and no autoscaling of batch work away from peak hours. If we bought more hardware tomorrow, we would very likely reproduce the same pattern: four new cards averaging 38% utilisation while our p95 latency still spikes at 2pm. When one option is a one-way door and the other is a revolving one, and we're genuinely uncertain which is right, the reversible path should win.

We've been hitting capacity ceilings on our local inference cluster during peak hours. Queue times for batch jobs have crept up, and interactive workloads occasionally degrade in ways that users notice. Two proposals are on the table. The first is to purchase additional accelerator hardware — roughly enough to add forty percent more raw capacity. The second is to invest engineering time in improving utilisation of the fleet we already own, through better scheduling, batching, quantisation of models where quality permits, and retiring the long tail of idle or lightly-used deployments.

**The cost picture**

The purchase option is straightforward to price: capital outlay, plus the ongoing costs of power, cooling, rack space, and the operational burden of managing more machines. What's harder to price is the depreciation risk. Accelerator hardware has historically held value poorly as new generations arrive, and anything we buy now will likely be worth a fraction of its cost in three years. The utilisation option, by contrast, costs mostly engineering time — perhaps six to eight weeks of focused work from two people. That's not free, but it's an expense we can dial up or down, and the skills and tooling we build along the way compound: a better scheduler or a cleaner batching pipeline keeps paying off regardless of how much hardware we own.

**Latency and reliability**

Utilisation work carries real risks here. Aggressive batching improves throughput but can add latency to interactive requests; quantisation trades some model quality for speed and memory. If we get these trade-offs wrong, we could solve our capacity problem while quietly degrading the user experience that made the service worth having. Buying hardware, in contrast, is almost risk-free from a quality standpoint — more capacity simply means queues shrink. On reliability, though, the picture inverts. Right now our fleet is already running hot at peak, and adding load-bearing complexity on top of strained hardware is how outages happen. More headroom, whether from new machines or from breathing room created by efficiency work, improves reliability either way — but the efficiency path gets us there while also reducing the number of moving parts, which arguably helps more.

**Opportunity cost**

This is where I think the decision actually turns. The engineers who would do the utilisation work are the same ones we'd need to integrate new hardware, migrate workloads, and re-tune everything afterward. Buying hardware doesn't save their time; it spends it differently, and probably on less interesting problems. Meanwhile, the utilisation work produces knowledge — about our actual workload shapes, our real quality tolerances, our peak patterns — that we currently lack and that any future purchasing decision should be based on. If we buy first and measure later, we may discover we bought the wrong thing, or bought twice as much as we needed. There's also a subtler opportunity cost: every dollar of capital committed to depreciating hardware is a dollar not available for the model experiments and product work that actually differentiate us.

**Reversibility**

The two options differ sharply here. Hardware purchases are nearly irreversible at our scale — resale markets for used accelerators are thin, and the money is gone. Utilisation work is highly reversible: if a quantised model disappoints, we roll back; if a scheduling change hurts latency, we revert. Reversible decisions deserve to be made first and cheaply; irreversible ones deserve to be made last and carefully, with the best information available.

Spend the next six weeks on utilisation before buying anything. Specifically, instrument the fleet properly, implement smarter batching and scheduling, quantise the two or three workloads where quality tolerance is known to be generous, and decommission what's idle. Then re-measure. My expectation is that we recover twenty-five to forty percent of effective capacity, which may be enough to defer purchase entirely — and if it isn't, we'll buy with a precise understanding of what we actually need, likely less than forty percent more, and with tooling that makes the new hardware genuinely useful on day one.

**Uncertainty**

I want to be honest about the limits of this reasoning. If our demand growth is steeper than current trends suggest, efficiency work only delays the inevitable purchase, and the delay has its own cost in user pain. If the team's time gets pulled into firefighting — a real risk given current load — the utilisation work could stall and leave us worse off than a decisive purchase would have. I'd therefore propose a checkpoint at week four: if measured gains are tracking below fifteen percent, or if the team is being consumed by incidents, we cut losses and proceed with procurement using whatever we've learned. That keeps the downside bounded while preserving the option value of the cheaper, smarter path.
